name: Cost of Capital
kick: valuation · risk as a number · the discount rate
title: Cost of capital — how risk shrinks the future into today's money
lede: A dollar in ten years is worth less than a dollar today. But by how much less? And when the business is riskier, shouldn't those future dollars count for even less? Here is how to put a number on risk, what happens when you change that number, why it is the most powerful lever in a valuation, and why this one number connects every company to interest rates and the market's mood.
arc: Why risk belongs in the rate

sections.h2: 1 · The problem — the future is less certain, so why is it worth the same?

blocks.html: Suppose a business will hand you $100 a year for the next ten years, and then it is worthless. You could add those up and say it is worth $1,000. But that is obviously wrong. A $100 bill sitting on a table now has more value to you than a $100 bill you will receive in year 10, because you could invest that $100 today and earn returns in the meantime. Even in a world with zero risk, the timing of cash matters.

Now add reality: the business is uncertain. The $100 might shrink if a competitor shows up. It might evaporate if the market cracks. The further out you look, the foggier it gets. So a dollar in year 10 is worth less than a dollar in year 1, not only because of time, but because you cannot trust it as much. The question is: how much less? By what fraction should you shrink each future dollar to make it comparable to a dollar you have today?

sections.h2: 2 · The reframe — pick a yearly shrinking rate that reflects the risk

blocks.html: Instead of trying to guess the odds of every possible future, you pick a single yearly discount rate — a percentage that says ‘each year that passes, shrink the value of future money by this much.’ A low rate means you trust the future. A high rate means you are nervous — risk is real, and distant cash counts for much less. The name for this rate, when you are valuing a company, is the cost of capital.

The logic is this: if you invest your money at a certain rate of return — say, in government bonds, which are almost riskless — then any investment you consider instead must offer you a higher return to make up for the extra risk you are taking. The cost of capital is that required return, built from three pieces: the risk-free rate (what you could earn on bonds), a risk premium (the extra percentage you demand for being brave), and a measure of how much riskier this particular business is than the average investment. Plug that rate into the valuation engine and you have discounted the future in a way that matches the real risk.

sections.h2: 3 · Seen on a real run — the same cash flows, worth very different amounts

blocks.html: We took our example company, Northwind, with its forecasted future cash, and asked: what is it worth if we discount at different cost-of-capital rates? Each rate tells a story about risk. The same company, same cash flows, radically different values.

blocks.caption: Identical future cash flows from Northwind, discounted at different yearly rates. A 5-point swing in the rate — from 7% to 12% — cuts the value in half.

blocks.html: The discovered fact: a higher discount rate shrinks the future into the present far more aggressively. Move the rate from 9% to 12% and the same company, with the same cash forecast, is worth less than 60% of its original value. The cost of capital is not a footnote in the spreadsheet — it is a lever that more than halves the answer across a plausible range.

sections.h2: 4 · Why risk belongs in the rate

blocks.html: Think of it this way. If you lend money to a government, you might accept a 2% yearly return because the money is safe. If you invest in a stable utility company, you might demand 6%, because there is some risk it stumbles. If you are backing a startup with a 50-50 shot at either tripling or vanishing, you should demand 30% or more, because most of the time you will lose.

The cost of capital is the rate that says: ‘based on how safe or risky I think this business is, this is the minimum return I need to make it worth my while to hand over my money.’ A risky business with predictable cash flows stays risky no matter what the cash looks like — the rate captures that. A safer business gets a lower rate and a higher value. That is the market at work: the more dangerous you think the future is, the more you charge for believing in it.

sections.h2: 5 · The one real weakness — the 'right' rate is itself a guess

blocks.html: Here is the uncomfortable truth: you cannot measure the cost of capital directly. It is an estimate, built from the risk-free rate (what do government bonds pay today?), a risk premium for investing in stocks at all (what extra percentage does history say you need to justify the risk?), and a beta — a number saying how much more or less volatile this particular company is than the stock market as a whole. Each of those three pieces is debatable.

So the cost of capital is not a fact. It is an educated guess about risk. And because a small change in this one number more than halves the value — as you saw in the run — a small change in your guess about risk quietly reprices everything. Pick 8% instead of 9% and you go from $53.75 to $43.23 — 20% less value, from a single number that you cannot even measure with confidence.

sections.h2: 6 · The surprise — this one number links the whole valuation to interest rates and market mood

blocks.html: Here is where it gets unsettling. Your company's value depends on the cost of capital. The cost of capital depends on the risk-free rate — what governments pay on bonds. The risk-free rate is set by the Federal Reserve, macro events, and inflation expectations. So when the Fed raises interest rates, every single valuation in the world drops, even if the company's future cash does not change one dollar. A rate hike is not a change in the business; it is a change in what you demand in return for risk.

That is why a rising interest rate environment can crash stock prices that have no reason to crash, and why a falling rate environment can inflate prices. The cost of capital ties every company back to the economy's mood about risk and reward. Learn this one number and you have learned why valuations move with interest rates, why recessions kill growth stocks first (their value lives far in the future and gets hit hardest by a higher discount rate), and why the moment the Fed starts cutting rates again, suddenly those companies look cheap again — not because their business changed, but because the rate did.

recipe.summary: A discounted-cash-flow engine on the example company Northwind: forecast free cash flow for 10 years from revenue growth, operating margin, tax, and reinvestment. Discount at different cost-of-capital rates (7%, 8%, 9%, 10%, 12%) and observe how the same future cash changes value based on the discount rate applied. Add a terminal value for the years beyond. Inputs are stated assumptions. numpy only.
recipe.eq:
value = sum( FCF_year / (1+cost_of_capital)^year ) + terminal_value / (1+cost_of_capital)^10
cost_of_capital = risk_free_rate + risk_premium + beta * (market_risk_premium)
# Northwind at 7%: $69.20, at 9%: $43.23, at 12%: $25.60 per share
recipe.note: Full engine: scripts/experiments/valuation_run.py (EXP3). Numbers are the run's output verbatim.
